That last step alone recovers 20-35% of no-shows. Most businesses simply mark the lead dead and move on, leaving paid traffic dollars on the floor. For reschedules, AI handles the back-and-forth with no human friction. The lead texts 'need to move,' the AI offers three new times, the lead picks, the calendar updates. Zero staff time. If you're running paid lead generation, plug this into your reporting: track booked, confirmed, showed, closed at every stage. The lift from AI confirmation typically pays for the entire system in the first 30 days.

Realistic ROI math and timelines

Stop reading vendor case studies. Run your own numbers. Take a service business doing 100 leads/month at a 30% booking rate and 50% show rate. That's 15 actual appointments. Move to AI setting with proper confirmation: 60% booking rate, 75% show rate. That's 45 appointments—3x the volume on the same ad spend. If your close rate is 25% on a $3,000 service, you've gone from $11,250 to $33,750 in monthly revenue. Software cost: ~$500/month. Setup cost: $3,000 one-time. Payback on a properly deployed AI setter is typically 14-45 days for businesses doing 50+ leads/month. Below that volume, the ROI is real but slower—and you may be better off with simpler automation (text-back, calendar links) before adding voice AI. Timeline expectations: - Week 1: Map flows, write scripts, configure CRM

  • Week 2: Build and test on a sandbox
  • Week 3: Soft launch on 25% of lead volume
  • Week 4-6: Iterate on transcripts, fix edge cases
  • Week 6+: Full deployment, kill the legacy process Budget 60-90 days for stable performance. Anyone promising 'plug and play in a day' is selling you a demo, not a system.

The bottom line

An AI appointment setter isn't a futuristic toy—it's the most underpriced operational upgrade available to small businesses right now. It replaces real headcount, recovers real revenue, and works the hours no human will. The businesses winning in the next 24 months are the ones that build this layer between marketing and sales before their competitors do. Start with a brutal audit of your current funnel: what's your speed-to-lead, your contact rate, your show rate, and your reschedule volume? If any of those numbers are embarrassing—and they probably are—you have a clear case to deploy AI before you hire the next SDR or front-desk admin.

faq.answer: Expect $300-$800/month in software (CRM, voice AI, SMS) plus $1,500-$5,000 one-time setup if you hire it built. Compared to a $60K+ SDR salary, payback is typically inside 60 days for businesses doing 50+ leads/month.

faq.question: Will leads know they're talking to an AI?
faq.answer: On SMS and web chat, most won't notice or care—the conversation feels normal. On voice calls, current AI voice quality (Vapi, Bland) is convincing for short interactions, but sophisticated leads can sometimes tell. Best practice is to be transparent if asked directly, and always allow a clean handoff to a human.

faq.question: Can AI handle complex qualification questions?
faq.answer: Yes, within limits. AI handles budget, timeline, service type, and decision-maker questions well. It struggles with nuanced pricing negotiation or highly technical specs. For tickets over $10K, use AI to qualify and book, then let a human closer handle the deal.

faq.question: What's the difference between an AI appointment setter and a chatbot?
faq.answer: A chatbot answers questions on your website. An AI appointment setter orchestrates conversations across web, SMS, and voice calls, integrates with your calendar and CRM, qualifies leads, books appointments, and handles confirmations and reschedules. It's a full workflow, not a Q&A widget.

faq.question: How long until an AI setter is fully running?
faq.answer: Plan for 4-6 weeks from kickoff to stable performance. Week one is mapping and scripts, weeks two through three are build and soft launch, and weeks four through six are iteration based on real conversation transcripts. Anyone promising same-day deployment is selling a demo.

articles.title: The Lead Follow Up Sequence That Books Service Appointments
articles.description: Most service businesses lose 60% of leads to slow follow-up. Here's the multi-touch SMS and email cadence that revives cold leads and books appointments.
articles.keyword: landing page conversion rate optimization for lead generation
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Speed-to-lead is the most underpriced advantage in service marketing. Research on more than a million leads found that reaching out within five minutes makes you 21x more likely to qualify a prospect than waiting 30 minutes. Yet the average service business — plumbers, law firms, med spas, contractors — takes over an hour to respond, if it responds at all.

The leak isn't your ad spend. It's the gap between when a lead raises their hand and when a human (or a well-built sequence) actually engages them. Every minute of silence is a lead drifting to the competitor who answered first.

This is the exact multi-touch follow-up cadence we deploy for service clients in GoHighLevel: SMS, email, and voicemail working together to revive cold leads and book appointments without your team chasing anyone. No new ad budget required — just stop letting paid leads die in a spreadsheet.

Why service leads go cold (and it's not the lead's fault)

A lead who fills out your form at 9:14 PM is not a bad lead. They're a hot lead you ignored until 11 AM the next day. By then they've filled out three more forms, taken a call from a competitor, and forgotten which company you even are.

Service buyers operate on urgency. A burst pipe, a car accident, a Botox appointment before a wedding — these aren't researched for weeks. The intent window is hours, sometimes minutes. Miss it and the lead doesn't 'go cold,' it goes to someone else.

The second killer is single-channel follow-up. Most businesses send one email, maybe one call, then quit. But it takes an average of 6 to 8 touches to convert a lead, and the businesses sending one or two are leaving the majority of their pipeline on the table. Your CRM is full of 'dead' leads that were never actually worked — they were tapped once and abandoned. The fix isn't more leads. It's a system that touches every lead, on every channel, until they book or explicitly opt out.

The five-minute speed-to-lead trigger

Touch number one fires automatically the instant a lead submits — not when your front desk gets to it. In GoHighLevel, the moment a form, Facebook lead ad, or Google Local Service Ad hits your pipeline, an automation sends an SMS within 60 seconds: 'Hi {first name}, this is Sarah from {company}. Saw you reached out about {service} — are you free for a quick call in the next hour?'

SMS, not email, leads the charge. Text messages carry a 98% open rate and a median response time under three minutes. Email opens average 20%. For a time-sensitive service inquiry, the channel choice alone can double your contact rate.

Simultaneously, fire an internal notification to the rep's phone so a human can call while the lead is still on your site. This is the highest-ROI automation a service business can build: the five-minute trigger routinely lifts lead-to-appointment rates 30–50% with zero added ad spend. If you build nothing else from this article, build this.

Days 1 to 3: the aggressive contact window

The first 72 hours decide most of your conversions, so the cadence should be dense without being spammy. Here's the structure we run:

Day 1: SMS at minute one (above) + a call attempt within five minutes + a follow-up email at hour two with social proof — a one-line case result and a Calendly or GHL booking link.

Day 2: A second call attempt in the morning, then an SMS in the early afternoon if no answer: 'Still want to help you with {service}, {first name}. Want me to hold a slot for tomorrow?' Afternoon contact windows (1–4 PM) consistently out-convert mornings for service replies.

Day 3: A value email — not another 'just checking in.' Send something useful: a pricing guide, a 'what to expect' breakdown, a financing option. This reframes you from pest to advisor.

The rule across all three days: every message names the service, includes a clear next step, and makes booking a one-tap action. Friction kills cadences faster than timing does.

Days 4 to 14: the nurture-and-revive cadence

If a lead hasn't booked by day three, they're not dead — they're busy, comparison shopping, or waiting on a decision-maker. Now the cadence stretches out and shifts from urgency to value.

Drop to one touch every two to three days, alternating SMS and email. The content rotates through proof and objection-handling: a Google review screenshot, a short before/after, an FAQ that quietly handles price ('Why our quote includes X when others charge extra'), and a soft-deadline offer if you run one ('We have two install slots left this week').

This is where ringless voicemail earns its keep. A 20-second voicemail drop — 'Hey {first name}, didn't want you to fall through the cracks, call me back when you get a sec' — feels personal and pulls a surprising number of replies precisely because nobody else is doing it. Tag any lead that clicks a link or replies as 'engaged' and route them back to a live rep immediately. The cadence exists to surface intent; humans close it.

Building it in GoHighLevel without a developer

You don't need custom code. The entire sequence lives in GoHighLevel's workflow builder, and you can stand up a working version in an afternoon.

Start with a single workflow triggered by 'Form Submitted' or 'Inbound Lead.' Add an SMS action at minute zero, a 'Wait' step, then branching email and SMS actions across the 14-day timeline. Use if/else conditions on appointment status so anyone who books is pulled out of the sequence instantly — nothing torches trust like getting a 'still interested?' text after you already scheduled.

Wire in three things that most setups skip: a missed-call-text-back automation (every unanswered call auto-sends an SMS), two-way SMS so replies land in a unified inbox your team actually watches, and a 'Stop on Reply' rule for compliance and sanity. Connect your calendar so booking links create real appointments, and pipe everything to a dashboard. If GHL isn't your stack, the same logic maps cleanly onto HubSpot workflows or a Zapier-plus-Twilio build — the platform matters far less than the cadence discipline.

The numbers that prove the sequence is working

A follow-up sequence you don't measure is just hope with extra steps. Track five metrics and the system becomes self-optimizing.

Speed-to-first-touch: median time from submission to first contact. Target under five minutes. If this creeps up, your automation broke — check it weekly. Contact rate: percent of leads you reach a human conversation with. A tuned cadence pushes this past 60%, versus the 20–30% most service businesses limp along with. Lead-to-appointment rate: the money metric. Expect 30–50% lifts after deploying the five-minute trigger alone.

Then watch touches-to-book (most appointments land between touch 4 and 7 — proof that quitting early costs you) and opt-out rate (keep it under 2%; higher means your cadence is too aggressive or your list is mistargeted). Review these in your GHL dashboard or Google Analytics every Monday. The sequence isn't 'set and forget' — it's 'set, measure, and sharpen.' The businesses that win aren't the ones with the cleverest copy. They're the ones who answer first and never stop following up.

The bottom line

Your competitors are buying the same leads from the same Meta and Google auctions you are. The difference between the business that scales and the one that plateaus isn't the cost per lead — it's what happens in the 14 days after the lead comes in. A disciplined, multi-channel follow-up sequence turns the leads you already pay for into booked revenue, automatically, while your team focuses on closing instead of chasing.

Build the five-minute trigger first. Layer in the day-1-to-3 contact window, then the day-4-to-14 nurture. Measure speed-to-touch and lead-to-appointment every week. Do that, and you'll wring 30–50% more appointments out of the exact same ad spend — which is the highest-leverage growth move most service businesses never make.

faq.question: How fast should I follow up with a new service lead?
faq.answer: Within five minutes, ideally within 60 seconds via automated SMS. Reaching a lead inside five minutes makes you roughly 21x more likely to qualify them than waiting 30 minutes. Build an automated first touch so speed never depends on whether your front desk is at their desk.

faq.question: How many times should I follow up before giving up?
faq.answer: At least 6 to 8 touches across 14 days. Most service appointments get booked between the 4th and 7th touch, yet the average business quits after one or two. A structured cadence that mixes SMS, email, and voicemail captures the majority of conversions that single-touch follow-up leaves behind.

faq.question: Should I use SMS or email for lead follow-up?
faq.answer: Both, but lead with SMS for the time-sensitive first 72 hours. Text messages get 98% open rates and replies in minutes; email opens average around 20%. Use SMS for urgency and quick booking, and email for longer-form proof, pricing guides, and objection-handling content.

faq.question: Can I build this follow-up sequence without a developer?
faq.answer: Yes. The entire cadence runs inside GoHighLevel's no-code workflow builder and can be live in an afternoon. The same logic also maps onto HubSpot workflows or a Zapier-plus-Twilio setup. What matters is the cadence discipline and clean if/else branching so booked leads exit the sequence automatically.

faq.question: How do I avoid annoying leads with too many messages?
faq.answer: Front-load the urgency (days 1–3), then stretch to one value-driven touch every 2–3 days. Always include a 'Stop on Reply' rule, honor opt-outs instantly, and pull anyone who books out of the sequence. Keep your opt-out rate under 2% — if it climbs higher, your cadence is too aggressive or your targeting is off.

articles.title: Lead Follow Up Sequence for Service Businesses That Books Jobs
articles.description: The exact 14-day SMS and email follow up sequence service businesses use to revive cold leads, book appointments, and lift close rates by 30%+.
articles.keyword: lead follow up sequence for service businesses
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's an uncomfortable number: 48% of inbound leads to service businesses never get a second contact attempt. Not because the leads are bad, but because the operator got busy, the rep forgot, or the CRM never fired the next message. Meanwhile, the data from Velocify and InsideSales shows that 50% of buyers go with the vendor who responds first — and the second-place finisher rarely gets a callback. If you run a home services company, an agency, a med spa, a law firm, or a lending shop, this is the single highest-ROI fix you can make this quarter. Not more ad spend. Not a new landing page. A documented, multi-touch SMS and email cadence that runs whether you're sleeping, in a sales meeting, or on a job site. Below is the exact sequence we deploy for clients — timing, channel, message templates, tooling, and the metrics that tell you it's working.

Why most service business follow up fails

Most operators think they have a follow up problem. They actually have a system problem. The typical service business flow looks like this: lead fills a form → goes to email inbox or a Google Sheet → owner or office manager calls when they can → if no answer, lead dies. One touch. Maybe two. The data is brutal: - 78% of sales go to the company that contacts the prospect first (InsideSales).

  • Leads contacted within 5 minutes are 100x more likely to convert than those contacted at 30 minutes (Harvard Business Review).
  • It takes an average of 6-8 touches to generate a viable sales lead (RAIN Group). So the company doing one phone call and one email is losing to the company doing eight touches across SMS, email, and voicemail — even if their offer is worse. The other failure mode is channel bias. Owners over 40 default to email. Leads under 40 ignore email. If your sequence doesn't hit SMS hard in the first 24 hours, you're talking to yourself. Open rates on SMS sit at 98% with a median response time under 90 seconds. Email opens hover at 21% for service verticals (Mailchimp benchmarks). Pick your weapon accordingly.

The 14-day cadence framework that works

Here's the skeleton we install in GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or ActiveCampaign for nearly every service client. It assumes a lead came in via web form, Meta lead ad, or Google LSA. Day 0 (within 5 minutes):

  1. Automated SMS: personal-sounding, references the service requested.
  2. Automated email: confirmation + calendar link (Calendly or built-in scheduler).
  3. Phone call from a human or AI voice agent. Day 0 (4 hours later, if no booking): Second SMS — soft check-in. Day 1: Email with social proof (review, case study, before/after). Day 2: Phone call attempt #2 + voicemail drop. Day 3: SMS with a specific question ("Still looking to get this handled before [month]?"). Day 5: Email — objection handler (price, timing, trust). Day 7: SMS — scarcity or scheduling nudge. Day 10: Phone call attempt #3. Day 14: Breakup email ("Closing your file unless I hear back"). That's 9 touches across 3 channels in 14 days. After Day 14, the lead drops into a long-term nurture (monthly email + quarterly SMS) for 12 months. Most operators stop at Day 2. The money is between Day 5 and Day 14.

The first 5 minutes: speed-to-lead automation

Speed-to-lead is the single biggest lever. A lead that waits 30 minutes for a response is functionally a different lead than one contacted in 5 minutes — they've already filled out three competitor forms. Here's the stack we use to hit 5-minute response on every lead, 24/7: - Lead capture: Meta Lead Ads, Google LSA, web form, or call tracking (CallRail).

  • Router: Zapier or native CRM webhook fires the moment the lead is created.
  • First SMS (instant): "Hey {firstName}, this is Sarah with {company}. Saw you requested a quote on {service} — got a sec to confirm a couple details?"
  • First email (instant): Subject: "{firstName}, your {service} quote" — body confirms the request, sets expectations, includes booking link.
  • First call (within 2 min): Either live rep, a power dialer like Aircall, or an AI voice agent (Air.ai, Bland, or GHL's built-in voice). The SMS does the heavy lifting. We see 40-60% reply rates on first-touch SMS when it's sent within 5 minutes and uses a real first name. Drop to 30 minutes and reply rate falls below 15%. The behavior change is non-linear — every minute of delay compounds. If you do nothing else from this article, install the instant SMS today.

SMS templates that don't sound automated

The fastest way to kill a sequence is sounding like a robot. Leads can smell merge tags and corporate-speak from a mile away. Rules we enforce on every client SMS: 1. Under 160 characters so it sends as a single segment. 2. No links in the first message (drives spam flags and lowers reply rate). 3. One question per message — never two. 4. Lowercase casual tone, contractions, occasional typo-style abbreviations. 5. Signed with a real first name, not the company name. Examples that consistently outperform: - Day 0: "hey {firstName} — sarah from {company}. saw your request for {service}. you around for a quick 2 min call to nail down pricing?"

  • Day 2: "{firstName} quick one — are you still looking to get {service} done in the next couple weeks, or should I close your file out?"
  • Day 7: "hey — got an opening tues at 10 or thurs at 2 if you want me to swing by for the estimate. either work?"
  • Day 14 (breakup): "sounds like the timings off — going to close your file. if anything changes shoot me a text. appreciate you {firstName}." The breakup message is the dark horse. We see 15-25% reply rates on it consistently. People who ignored you for two weeks suddenly engage when they think the door is closing.

Email sequences that handle objections before they're spoken

Email isn't dead for service businesses — it's just misused. Email is where you do the heavy lifting on trust and objections that SMS can't carry. Your 4-email sequence inside the 14 days should each tackle one specific objection: Email 1 (Day 0) — Confirmation + expectation set. "Here's what happens next, here's our process, here's your booking link." Plain text, signed by a human, no headers or logos. Email 2 (Day 1) — Social proof. One specific case study or review with numbers. "We did {service} for {customer} in {neighborhood} last month — here's what they said." Include a photo if possible. Email 3 (Day 5) — Objection handler. Address the #1 reason your leads don't buy. For lenders, that's rates. For contractors, that's price. For agencies, that's results timeline. Be direct: "You're probably wondering about price. Here's how we think about it." Email 4 (Day 14) — Breakup. "Going to close your file. If timing changes, here's my direct number." Keep every email under 150 words, plain text, no HTML templates. We A/B tested fancy designed emails against plain text in HubSpot across 12 service accounts — plain text won on reply rate every single time, often by 2-3x.

The tools and stack to run this on autopilot

You don't need a 12-tool stack. You need 3-4 things that talk to each other. The minimum viable stack: - CRM + automation: GoHighLevel ($97-297/mo) is purpose-built for this and includes SMS, email, calls, and pipelines in one. HubSpot Starter works too but SMS requires add-ons.

  • Scheduling: Calendly or GHL's built-in calendar. Round-robin if you have multiple reps.
  • Call tracking + dialer: CallRail for tracking, Aircall or JustCall for outbound. If you're solo, use the CRM's mobile app.
  • AI voice (optional but powerful): Air.ai, Bland, or Synthflow for after-hours and unanswered call follow up. Adds 10-20% to bookings for most service clients. What to skip: Don't buy Salesforce. Don't buy Marketo. Don't build a custom Twilio integration unless you have an engineering team. The off-the-shelf tools are good enough and you'll launch in days instead of months. Setup time: A competent operator can build this in GoHighLevel in 6-10 hours. An agency can do it for you in a week. Either way, this is a one-time build with monthly tweaks based on reply data — not an ongoing 40-hour-a-week project.

Metrics that tell you the sequence is working

If you can't measure it, you can't fix it. Here are the only numbers that matter once your sequence is live. Top of funnel:

  • Speed to first touch — target under 5 minutes, 24/7.
  • SMS reply rate on Touch 1 — target 35%+.
  • Email open rate — target 40%+ on plain text. Middle of funnel:
  • Lead-to-booked-appointment rate — target 25-40% for inbound leads.
  • Touches-to-booking — most bookings happen between touches 3 and 6. If yours all come from touch 1, your follow up is weak. If they all come from touch 8+, your first message is weak. Bottom of funnel:
  • Booked-to-show rate — target 70%+ with SMS reminders at 24h and 1h before.
  • Show-to-close rate — this is your sales team, not the sequence.
  • Cost per booked appointment — divide ad spend by booked appointments. This is the number to obsess over. Review these weekly in a simple Google Sheet or your CRM dashboard. The sequence is a living document — kill the messages with under 5% engagement and double down on the ones pulling 30%+. Expect to iterate for the first 60 days before the cadence is dialed.

The bottom line

The service businesses winning right now aren't the ones with the best website or the cheapest CPL. They're the ones who contact every lead within 5 minutes and follow up 9 times over 14 days across SMS, email, and phone — without a human having to remember. That's it. That's the whole game. Your next action: pull your last 30 days of leads, count how many got more than two follow up attempts, and calculate what your close rate would look like at 8 touches instead of 2. That number is what this sequence is worth to your business. Build it this week.

faq.question: How many times should I follow up with a lead before giving up?
faq.answer: Minimum 8-9 touches across 14 days, then drop into long-term nurture for 12 months. Most service businesses stop at 2 touches and leave 40-60% of revenue on the table. The breakup message at Day 14 alone recovers 15-25% of cold leads.

faq.question: Is SMS or email better for service business lead follow up?
faq.answer: SMS for speed and response — 98% open rate and 90-second median reply time. Email for trust-building and objection handling. You need both: SMS in the first 24 hours to start a conversation, email throughout the 14 days to handle objections and provide social proof.

faq.question: What's the best tool to automate lead follow up for a service business?
faq.answer: GoHighLevel for most service businesses under $5M in revenue — it bundles SMS, email, calls, scheduling, and pipelines for $97-297/month. HubSpot works if you're already on it but SMS requires add-ons. Avoid Salesforce and Marketo unless you have enterprise needs.

faq.question: How fast do I need to respond to a new lead?
faq.answer: Under 5 minutes, 24/7. Leads contacted within 5 minutes are 100x more likely to convert than those contacted at 30 minutes. After-hours response requires automation — instant SMS and email, plus an AI voice agent or scheduled call-back for the morning.

faq.question: Won't aggressive follow up annoy my leads and hurt my brand?
faq.answer: No, if the messages are short, conversational, and ask one question at a time. The leads who unsubscribe weren't going to buy anyway. The leads who book on touch 5 or 7 weren't ignoring you — they were busy. Persistence with good copy reads as professionalism, not annoyance.

articles.title: Why Am I Not Getting Leads From Facebook Ads? 7 Real Fixes
articles.description: No leads from Facebook ads? Here are the 7 usual culprits, how to diagnose which one is killing your campaign, and the exact order to fix them in.
articles.keyword: how to get more leads for a service business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
If you are asking why am I not getting leads from Facebook ads, the honest answer is almost never "Facebook is broken." Meta runs four million advertisers and still delivers some of the cheapest qualified attention on the internet. The platform is doing its job. Something upstream of the click, or downstream of it, is leaking.

The trap is that "no leads" feels like one problem. It is actually seven possible problems wearing the same costume. Pour more budget into a campaign with a broken landing page and you simply buy more expensive silence. Swap creative when the real issue is your offer and you waste a week chasing the wrong variable.

This is the diagnostic we run on every underperforming account before we touch a single dial. Work it in order, top to bottom, because each layer depends on the one above it. Fix the objective before you blame the creative. Fix the offer before you blame the audience.

Start with the campaign objective, not the creative

The single most common reason a service business gets zero leads is that the campaign was never asking for leads. We constantly audit accounts running Traffic or Engagement objectives and wondering why the form never fills. Meta optimizes for exactly what you tell it to. Ask for clicks and it finds the cheapest clickers on the platform, who are rarely buyers.

Open Meta Ads Manager and check the objective column. For lead generation you want Leads (with either an Instant Form or a website conversion event) or Sales if you are sending traffic to a booking page that fires a Lead or Schedule event. Anything else is the wrong tool.

Then check the optimization event one level down at the ad set. Even on a Leads campaign, if you are optimizing for Landing Page Views instead of the actual Lead event, Meta hunts for browsers, not submitters. This one misconfiguration accounts for more "Facebook doesn't work for me" complaints than every other cause combined. Fix it first, because nothing below this line matters if the algorithm is optimizing toward the wrong human.

Confirm your pixel and conversion event actually fire

Here is the silent killer: your campaign is set to optimize for Leads, but Meta has never once received a Lead event, so it is flying blind and spending randomly. If the pixel is broken, the smartest optimization objective in the world has no signal to learn from.

Install the Meta Pixel Helper Chrome extension and load your landing page and thank-you page. You should see the base PageView fire everywhere and a single Lead or CompleteRegistration event fire only after a form submit. Two fires, missing fires, or a Lead event firing on page load all corrupt your data.

Cross-check in Events Manager under the Test Events tab, then submit a real test lead and watch it appear within seconds. If you run GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or a native form, verify the Conversions API connection too, since iOS signal loss means browser-pixel-only tracking now undercounts conversions by 20 to 40 percent. Broken tracking is invisible in the ad account, which is why teams burn thousands before catching it. Verify signal before you blame anything creative.

Audit the audience: too narrow, too broad, or just wrong

Once the plumbing is sound, look at who you are reaching. Audience problems show up in two opposite shapes. Too narrow, and Meta cannot exit the learning phase, your frequency spikes within days, and CPMs climb as you fight for a tiny pool. Too broad with weak creative, and you pay to reach people who will never care.

In 2026, Meta's delivery system rewards breadth. For most service businesses, a broad audience (age, gender, wide geo, no interest stacking) plus strong creative outperforms the hyper-layered interest targeting that worked in 2019. The creative is now the targeting. Let the algorithm find buyers using your messaging as the filter.

The exception is local service businesses. If you serve a 25-mile radius, your geo IS your constraint, and you must feed Meta enough budget to actually saturate that area, or it will never stabilize. Check your audience size estimate: under roughly 200,000 people for a conversion campaign and you are probably starving the algorithm of room to optimize.

Your creative is the real targeting now

If the objective is right, tracking fires, and the audience is sane, creative is your next suspect, and statistically your most likely one. Meta's own data shows creative drives the majority of performance variance between ads. A boring ad to a perfect audience loses to a scroll-stopping ad to a broad one.

Diagnose with two numbers in Ads Manager: CTR (link click-through rate) and hook rate (3-second video views divided by impressions). A link CTR under roughly 1 percent means the creative is not earning the click. A low hook rate means people scroll past in the first second, so the rest of the ad never gets a chance.

Fix it with volume and variety, not polish. Run four to six distinct creative concepts, not four versions of the same image with different fonts. Test a raw UGC-style video, a bold text-on-image static, a customer result, and a direct problem-callout. Native, slightly imperfect creative consistently beats over-produced agency gloss because it does not look like an ad. The goal is to stop the thumb.

The offer matters more than the ad

You can have flawless tracking, a broad audience, and a thumb-stopping video, and still get zero leads if the offer is weak. This is the layer most people skip because it is uncomfortable: sometimes the market is telling you the thing you are selling, at the price and risk you are asking, is not worth the click.

A strong offer reduces risk and increases specificity. "Get a free quote" is not an offer; it is a chore, and it competes with every other business asking the same. "Free 20-minute roof inspection with same-day written estimate, no obligation" is an offer, because it is specific, time-bound, and removes the fear of a hard sell.

Ask what the prospect gets, how fast, and what it costs them in time or risk to say yes. Lead magnets, free assessments, instant quotes, and guarantees all lower the activation energy. If your cost per lead is brutal across multiple good creatives, stop blaming the ads. The market is voting on your offer, and you should listen.

Diagnose the landing page and form friction

Plenty of campaigns generate clicks and still report no leads, because the leak is after the click. If your CTR is healthy but your cost per lead is awful, the landing page or form is where prospects quietly leave.

Pull the funnel apart. In Google Analytics or your landing page tool, compare clicks to page views (catch slow loads and tracking gaps), page views to form starts (catch weak page copy), and form starts to submissions (catch a form that asks too much). Each drop-off points to a different fix.

The usual offenders: a page that takes more than three seconds to load on mobile, where the vast majority of Meta traffic lives; a form demanding eight fields when three would do; a headline that does not match the ad, breaking the promise that earned the click; or no visible trust signals. Consider Meta Instant Forms to remove the landing page entirely for top-of-funnel volume. Match the page to the ad, cut every non-essential field, and test it on your own phone before spending another dollar.

Follow-up speed and creative fatigue: the final 20 percent

Two issues round out the diagnostic. First, follow-up. You may be getting leads and not realizing they are dying in the gap between submit and contact. Lead response research is brutally consistent: contacting a lead within five minutes versus thirty can lift connection rates by orders of magnitude. If a human cannot respond instantly, automate the first touch. A GoHighLevel or HubSpot workflow that texts and emails within sixty seconds, plus a Calendly link to self-book, recovers leads you are otherwise paying for and ignoring.

Second, fatigue. A campaign that worked for weeks and then died is usually not broken; it is tired. Check frequency in Ads Manager. Above roughly 3 to 4 within a week for a cold audience, your CTR drops and CPMs rise as the same people see the same ad repeatedly. The fix is a steady supply of fresh creative, not a budget increase. Build a simple production cadence so you always have the next concept ready before the current one burns out.

The bottom line

When leads dry up, resist the urge to yank random levers. Run the diagnostic in order: objective, tracking, audience, creative, offer, landing page, then follow-up and fatigue. Each layer sits on the one above it, so a fix lower down cannot save a break higher up. Nine times out of ten the culprit is one or two of these, not all seven, and once you find it the account turns quickly.

The operators who win on Meta are not the ones with secret targeting tricks. They are the ones with clean tracking, a strong offer, a steady supply of native creative, and instant follow-up. Get those four right and Facebook ads stop being a mystery and start being a predictable lead machine.

faq.question: How long should I run a Facebook ad before deciding it failed?
faq.answer: Give a campaign at least 7 days and roughly 50 optimization events (lead conversions) before judging it, so Meta can exit the learning phase. Killing ad sets after two days of low volume resets learning and guarantees instability. The exception is a clearly broken setup, like a misfiring pixel or wrong objective, which you should fix immediately rather than wait out.

faq.question: Why am I getting clicks but no leads from Facebook ads?
faq.answer: Clicks without leads almost always means the leak is after the click. Check landing page load speed on mobile, whether your form asks for too many fields, and whether the page headline matches the ad promise. Also confirm your Lead event actually fires on submit, since broken tracking can hide real leads that are coming through.

faq.question: Is a broad or narrow audience better for lead generation in 2026?
faq.answer: For most service businesses, broad targeting plus strong creative now beats narrow interest stacking. Meta's delivery system finds buyers using your creative as the filter. The main exception is local businesses, where your geographic radius is the real constraint and you must fund it enough to saturate the area.

faq.question: How much should I budget to know if Facebook ads work for my business?
faq.answer: A reasonable test budget is enough to generate about 50 conversions at your expected cost per lead within 7 to 14 days. If you expect a 30-dollar cost per lead, budget for roughly 1,500 dollars to gather meaningful signal. Under-funding the test starves the algorithm and produces noisy data you cannot trust.

faq.question: Could my offer be the reason I get no leads, even with good ads?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is one of the most overlooked causes. If your cost per lead stays high across several strong creatives and a clean funnel, the market is voting against your offer. Make it specific, time-bound, and low-risk. A vague free quote underperforms a concrete, guaranteed, fast outcome nearly every time.

articles.title: Why Am I Not Getting Leads From Facebook Ads? 7 Real Reasons
articles.description: Your Facebook ads aren't generating leads? Here are the 7 culprits killing your campaigns — and how to diagnose exactly which one is yours.
articles.keyword: why am I not getting leads from Facebook ads
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Roughly 62% of small businesses say their Facebook ads fail to deliver leads, according to WordStream's most recent benchmark data. Most of them blame the platform. Almost none of them are right. Facebook (Meta) still drives some of the cheapest qualified leads in paid media — we routinely see $8–$22 lead costs for service businesses, lenders, and agencies when the setup is dialed in. When it doesn't work, the failure is almost always traceable to one of seven specific causes. Not bad luck. Not iOS 14. Not the algorithm hating you. This article walks through every culprit, in the order you should diagnose them, with the exact signals to look for in Meta Ads Manager and what to fix first.

Culprit 1: You picked the wrong campaign objective

This is the most common and most expensive mistake. If you're running a Traffic or Engagement objective and wondering why leads aren't coming in, Meta is doing exactly what you asked: sending you clicks and likes, not buyers. Meta's algorithm optimizes for the specific event you tell it to optimize for. Tell it to find people who click, and it finds the cheapest clickers — typically low-intent users who scroll a lot. Tell it to find people who submit a lead form or trigger a Lead event via the Conversions API, and it goes hunting for a completely different audience. The fix: - For instant forms on Meta, use the Leads objective with the Instant Form conversion location.

  • For landing page submissions, use the Sales or Leads objective with a Lead or Purchase event fired via the Pixel + Conversions API.
  • Never run cold traffic campaigns on the Traffic objective and expect leads. It's a diagnostic tool at best. Check the "Performance Goal" column in Ads Manager. If it says "Maximize number of link clicks" or "landing page views," that's your problem. Duplicate the campaign, switch to Leads or Sales, and let it re-learn for 7 days before judging it.

Culprit 2: Your audience is too narrow, too broad, or just wrong

Most advertisers get audience wrong in one of two directions. They either stack 14 interests, two custom audiences, and a lookalike into one ad set (suffocating delivery), or they go fully broad with no signals and let Meta burn budget on toddlers and retirees. The 2024–2026 reality: Meta's targeting works best when you give it room to learn. Broad targeting (age + gender + country, no interests) often beats narrow stacks for cold acquisition — but only if your creative does the targeting work for you. Diagnostic steps: 1. Check audience size. For lead gen in the US, you want 1M–10M for interest-based and 5M+ for broad. 2. Look at the Audience breakdown by age and gender. If 60% of spend is going to 18–24 year olds and you sell to homeowners, your creative is attracting the wrong avatar. 3. Are you excluding existing leads and customers? Upload your CRM list (HubSpot, GoHighLevel, etc.) as a Custom Audience and exclude it from cold campaigns. The fix: Run a broad audience with sharper creative that calls out your buyer in the first 3 seconds ("Roofing contractors in Texas — read this"). Let the creative filter, not the targeting.

Culprit 3: Your creative is the actual problem (it usually is)

Creative drives 60–70% of paid social performance. If your CTR is below 1% and your CPM is above $40, your creative is the bottleneck — not your targeting, not your bidding. Go into Ads Manager and pull these columns: CTR (link click-through rate), Hook rate (3-sec video views ÷ impressions), Hold rate (ThruPlays ÷ 3-sec views), and Cost per lead. Here's what good looks like for service businesses: - CTR: 1.5%+

  • Hook rate: 25%+
  • Hold rate: 15%+
  • Frequency: under 2.5 in the first 14 days If your hook rate is under 20%, your first 3 seconds are dead. If your CTR is under 1%, your offer or message isn't landing. If hold rate is fine but CTR is low, you've got an offer/CTA problem. What's working in 2026: - Founder-shot UGC with text overlays (not polished brand video)
  • Direct, problem-aware hooks: "If your ads aren't getting leads, it's one of these 7 things"
  • Static images with bold, scroll-stopping copy beat fancy motion graphics for lead gen
  • 4–6 creative variants per ad set, refreshed every 2–3 weeks If you're running the same two ads you launched 60 days ago, that's also why.

Culprit 4: Your offer is forgettable

"Schedule a free consultation" is not an offer. It's a chore. If your CTA asks the prospect to give up 30 minutes of their life for vague value, expect a 0.5% conversion rate. A strong offer makes the next step feel like the prospect is getting away with something. Compare these: - Weak: "Book a free strategy call"

  • Strong: "Get the 14-point Facebook ad audit we use on $50k/mo accounts — free PDF, no call required" - Weak: "Apply for funding"
  • Strong: "See how much you pre-qualify for in 60 seconds. Soft pull, no impact to credit." Offer audit questions: 1. Is the value crystal clear in under 5 seconds?
  1. Is the friction (time, info required, perceived risk) low?
  2. Is there a reason to act now, not later?
  3. Does it match the awareness level of cold traffic? Cold Facebook traffic is problem-aware at best. They aren't ready to talk to sales. Lead magnets, calculators, audits, and quizzes consistently outperform "book a call" CTAs by 3–5x in cost per lead for cold campaigns. Save the call CTA for retargeting.

Culprit 5: Your landing page is leaking leads

You can have a perfect ad and still get zero leads if the landing page is broken. The benchmark for a paid-traffic lead gen landing page is a 15–30% conversion rate. Under 10% and you have a page problem. Plug your URL into PageSpeed Insights first. If mobile load time is over 3 seconds, you're losing 40%+ of clicks before they even see the form. Meta traffic is 90%+ mobile. Common landing page killers: - Form has 7+ fields (cut to name, email, phone, one qualifier)

  • Headline doesn't match the ad's promise (scent break)
  • Video autoplay with sound on
  • Cookie banners and chat widgets blocking the CTA on mobile
  • No social proof above the fold
  • Generic stock photos instead of real outcomes Check your funnel in Google Analytics 4 or GoHighLevel. If 200 people clicked the ad, 180 landed on the page, and only 4 submitted the form, the page is the leak — not the ads. Fast fixes: Match the H1 to the ad headline word-for-word. Cut the form fields in half. Add three customer quotes with photos. Remove every link in the nav. A landing page should have one job and one exit: submit or leave.

Culprit 6: Your follow-up is so slow the leads die

Here's a stat that should hurt: leads contacted within 5 minutes are 100x more likely to convert than leads contacted after 30 minutes (InsideSales / Harvard Business Review). Most service businesses respond in 24–48 hours, if at all. If you're "not getting leads from Facebook ads," check first whether you're getting leads and just losing them. Pull your CRM. Count submissions from the last 30 days. Cross-reference with how many were actually called or emailed within 10 minutes. Build this stack: 1. Instant lead capture — Meta Lead Ads → Zapier or native CRM integration → GoHighLevel/HubSpot. Don't rely on the CSV download from Ads Manager. People forget. Leads rot. 2. Speed-to-lead automation — SMS within 60 seconds ("Hey [Name], saw you requested the [offer]. Got 2 minutes?"), email within 5, call within 10. 3. 5–7 touch cadence over 14 days — most conversions happen on touches 3–5, not touch 1. 4. Calendly or GoHighLevel calendar embedded in the first SMS so they can self-book. If your follow-up game is weak, doubling ad spend just creates more wasted leads. Fix the back end before scaling the front.

Culprit 7: Ad fatigue is silently killing your account

Even great campaigns die. Frequency creeps up, CTR drops, CPL doubles, and suddenly the ads that worked in month one are bleeding money in month three. Watch these signals in Ads Manager: - Frequency above 3.0 in a 7-day window — your audience is seeing the same ad too often

  • CTR declining 20%+ week over week while CPM stays flat
  • CPL rising while conversion rate on the landing page stays steady — that means the ads are attracting worse leads, not the page failing
  • Negative feedback score trending toward "Below Average" in the Account Quality dashboard The cure is structural, not tactical: 1. Plan to refresh creative every 2–3 weeks for evergreen campaigns. Build a content engine, not one-off ads.
  1. Run a 3-3-3 testing structure: 3 new hooks, 3 new angles, 3 new formats per month.
  2. Separate cold prospecting from retargeting campaigns. Different creative, different frequency caps.
  3. Use Advantage+ Creative sparingly — it can mask which variants are actually winning. Fatigue isn't a sign Facebook ads stopped working. It's a sign your creative pipeline isn't keeping up with the platform's appetite.

How to diagnose which culprit is yours in 20 minutes

Don't guess. Work the funnel top to bottom: 1. Objective check (1 min): Is it Leads or Sales? If not, that's your answer. 2. Audience check (3 min): Look at age/gender/placement breakdowns. Does delivery match your buyer? 3. Creative check (5 min): Pull CTR, hook rate, hold rate. Anything red? That's your answer. 4. Offer check (2 min): Read your ad as a stranger. Would you click? 5. Landing page check (5 min): Run PageSpeed Insights, count form fields, check the headline match. 6. Follow-up check (3 min): Pull last 20 leads. Were they contacted in under 10 minutes? 7. Fatigue check (1 min): Frequency over 3? CTR trending down? Refresh creative. Nine times out of ten, you'll find the issue in the first three steps. The other one out of ten is a stack of two or three smaller leaks compounding.

The bottom line

"Facebook ads don't work" is almost never true. "Facebook ads don't work the way I'm running them" is true constantly. The seven culprits — objective, audience, creative, offer, landing page, follow-up, fatigue — cover roughly 95% of underperforming accounts we audit. Pick one. Diagnose with real numbers from Ads Manager, GA4, and your CRM. Fix it. Give the campaign 5–7 days to re-stabilize. Then move to the next leak. Most accounts can double lead volume in 30 days without spending an extra dollar — they just need to stop bleeding at the seams.

faq.question: How long should I run a Facebook ad campaign before deciding it's not working?
faq.answer: Give a new campaign at least 5–7 days and 50+ conversions to exit the learning phase before judging it. Killing ads after 48 hours based on a $30 spend is the fastest way to never find a winner. If you can't afford to spend $500–$1,500 on a real test, your budget is too small for Meta to optimize against.

faq.question: What's a realistic cost per lead on Facebook ads in 2026?
faq.answer: It depends entirely on industry and offer. Local service businesses typically see $8–$30 per lead, B2B SaaS $40–$120, lenders and financial services $15–$60, and high-ticket coaching $25–$80. If your CPL is 2–3x the industry benchmark, you have a fixable problem — not a platform problem.

faq.question: Should I use Meta Instant Forms or send traffic to a landing page?
faq.answer: Instant Forms produce 2–4x more leads at lower CPL, but lead quality is usually lower because of the friction-free submission. Landing pages produce fewer, higher-intent leads. For high-volume top-of-funnel, use Instant Forms with qualifying questions. For higher-ticket offers or sales calls, send to a landing page.

faq.question: Why did my Facebook ads stop working after they were doing great?
faq.answer: Almost always ad fatigue. Frequency climbs above 3, the same audience has seen your creative too many times, and performance decays. Refresh creative every 2–3 weeks, expand or rotate audiences, and separate cold from retargeting campaigns. The account isn't broken — the creative pipeline stalled.

faq.question: Can I run Facebook ads without a landing page?
faq.answer: Yes — use Meta Instant Forms (Lead Ads) and pipe submissions directly into your CRM via native integration or Zapier. This works well for top-of-funnel lead capture. For anything requiring more education or higher commitment, a dedicated landing page will outperform forms on lead quality.

articles.title: Best Lead Generation Companies for Contractors (2026)
articles.description: We ranked the best lead generation companies for contractors, then showed why renting leads quietly bleeds margin and what to build instead.
articles.keyword: AI receptionist for small business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most contractors don't have a lead problem. They have a lead ownership problem. They're paying Angi, Thumbtack, and a half-dozen pay-per-lead marketplaces $50 to $300 a pop for a phone number that three competitors bought at the same time.

The marketplaces aren't evil. They're just structurally aligned against you: the more they sell the same lead, the more revenue they make. That's not a partnership, that's a toll booth. Below we rank the platforms that actually move the needle for contractors, then make the uncomfortable case for why the smartest operators are quietly building the thing the marketplaces never want them to own.

The two ways contractors buy leads

Every contractor lead source falls into one of two buckets, and confusing them is why margins disappear.

Rented leads are pay-per-lead (PPL) marketplaces: Angi, Thumbtack, Networx, Modernize, 33 Mile Radius, CraftJack. You pay per contact, the platform owns the customer relationship, and the same lead is frequently sold to 3–5 of your competitors. You're renting access, and the rent never stops.

Owned leads come from a funnel you control: your website, your Meta and Google Ads, your Local Service Ads, your database. The cost-per-lead is often higher to acquire the first time, but the lead is exclusively yours, the second job from that customer costs nothing, and the asset compounds.

The ranking below covers the best rented-lead companies because you'll likely use them to bridge cash flow. But read the final sections before you build your whole business on someone else's platform. The contractors clearing 25%+ net margins are almost never the ones living inside a marketplace.

Best pay-per-lead marketplaces, ranked

Based on lead exclusivity, intent quality, and contractor-reported close rates, here's the honest tier list.

1. Google Local Service Ads (LSA). Not a marketplace in the classic sense, but the best PPL value for contractors, period. You pay per lead (not per click), get the Google Guaranteed badge, and leads come from people searching with high intent. Close rates of 20–40% are common. Disputes for junk leads are actually honored.

2. Angi (formerly Angie's List + HomeAdvisor). Massive volume, strong brand recall with homeowners. The catch: leads are typically shared, and quality swings hard by trade and ZIP. Works best for high-ticket trades (roofing, remodels) where one close pays for many leads.

3. Thumbtack. Better for smaller jobs and newer businesses. You set targeting tightly and only pay when a customer reaches out. Lead quality is mid, but the controls are good.

4. Modernize / Networx / CraftJack. Solid for specific verticals (windows, solar, HVAC). Exclusive-lead options exist at a premium and are worth it.

Use these to fill calendar gaps, not to define your business.

The true long-run cost of renting leads

Here's the math marketplaces never put on the homepage.

Say you pay $80 per shared lead and close 1 in 5. Your effective cost per acquired customer is $400. Run 200 leads a month and you're spending $16,000 to acquire 40 customers. Fine, until you realize you'll pay that same $400 to reach that same homeowner again next year, because the marketplace owns the relationship and remarkets to them.

Now model an owned funnel. The first customer might cost $450 to acquire through Meta and Google. But you captured their email and phone in your CRM (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or Jobber). The follow-up maintenance job, the referral, the review that brings two more — those cost you near zero. Over three years your blended cost-per-customer drops below $150.

The marketplace path is a flat line: you pay full freight forever. The owned path is a decay curve: cost drops as your database grows. After 18–24 months, owned almost always wins. Renting leads feels cheaper because the pain is spread across small monthly invoices. It's the most expensive cheap thing in contracting.

What an owned contractor funnel actually looks like

You don't need a marketing degree. You need five components wired together.

1. A conversion-first site. Not a brochure. One headline, proof (reviews, photos, license/insurance), and a form or call button above the fold. Speed matters: a 1-second delay can cut conversions noticeably.

2. Paid traffic you control. Google Search and LSA for people actively looking; Meta Ads for demand-gen in your service radius. Start with one channel, master it, then add.

3. Instant lead response. 78% of customers buy from the company that responds first. An automated text-back within 60 seconds (via GoHighLevel or similar) beats a competitor who calls back in two hours.

4. A CRM + database. Every lead, won or lost, lives in your system. This is the asset. Marketplaces never let you keep it.

5. A reactivation engine. Email and SMS to past customers for maintenance, seasonal offers, and referral asks. This is the highest-ROI line item in contracting and it costs almost nothing.

That's it. Five pieces. The marketplaces sell you piece two and keep the other four for themselves.

When marketplaces still make sense

This isn't a religion. Rented leads have a real, legitimate place in a contractor's mix.

You're brand new and need cash flow now. An owned funnel takes 60–90 days to hit stride. Marketplaces turn on today. Use them to keep crews busy while you build.

You have idle capacity. If your crew has open hours, a $400 acquired customer at 25% margin still prints money. Filling a truck beats an empty one.

You're testing a new trade or market. Buying leads in a new ZIP is a cheap way to validate demand before you spend on ads and SEO there.

Your trade has spiky, unpredictable demand. Restoration, emergency plumbing — marketplace volume can smooth the valleys.

The rule: rent leads to bridge, never to build. Cap marketplace spend at a fixed percentage of revenue — many smart operators hold it under 20% — and pour the rest into owned channels. Treat every marketplace dollar as a loan against the database you're not building. Over time, the goal is to need them less, not more.

How to vet a lead gen company before you spend

Before you hand any company a credit card, run this checklist. It filters out 90% of the regret.

Are the leads exclusive or shared? Shared isn't disqualifying, but it must be priced accordingly. Always ask how many contractors receive the same lead.

What's the refund/dispute policy on junk leads? Wrong numbers, out-of-area, tire-kickers — you'll get them. A company that won't credit obvious garbage is telling you who they serve.

Can you control trade, ZIP, and job type targeting? No granular targeting means you'll pay for leads you can't service.

Do you keep the customer data? Critical. If the answer is no, you're renting, full stop. Price it like rent.

Is there a contract or spend minimum? Month-to-month with no minimum is the safe starting posture. Avoid annual lock-ins until you've proven the channel.

What do real contractors in your trade say? Not testimonials on their site — actual operators in trade Facebook groups and Reddit. Quality varies wildly by vertical and region.

Run every platform — including the ones we ranked — through this gauntlet. The answers tell you whether you're buying a tool or signing up to be the product.

The play: a hybrid that compounds

Here's what we put in front of contractor clients at Social Elite Marketing Group, and it's not a pitch for any single platform.

Phase 1 (Months 0–2): Buy to bridge. Turn on Google LSA first — best risk-adjusted value. Add one marketplace (Angi or Thumbtack) capped at a fixed monthly budget. Goal: keep crews fed while you build.

Phase 2 (Months 1–4): Build the owned engine. Conversion site, Google Search ads, GoHighLevel CRM with 60-second text-back, and every lead — marketplace or organic — captured in your database. Now even your rented leads start building an owned asset.

Phase 3 (Months 3+): Shift the mix. As owned cost-per-customer drops, reallocate budget from marketplaces to ads, SEO, and reactivation. Most contractors flip from ~70% rented to ~70% owned within two quarters.

Phase 4 (Ongoing): Mine the database. Reactivation campaigns to past customers, referral systems, review generation. This is where margin lives and where marketplaces can never follow you.

The best lead gen company for contractors, long term, is the one you own. Everything else is a bridge to get there.

The bottom line

Rank the marketplaces all you want — Google LSA, Angi, Thumbtack, Modernize each have a real seat at the table. But the ranking that actually decides your margin isn't which company you rent from. It's whether you're building an asset or paying a toll forever.

Rent leads to bridge cash flow and fill idle capacity. Build an owned funnel — site, ads, CRM, instant response, reactivation — to compound. Do both at once, then shift the mix toward ownership every quarter. That's how contractors go from chasing the same shared lead as three competitors to owning a database that feeds itself.

faq.question: What is the best lead generation company for contractors?
faq.answer: For risk-adjusted value, Google Local Service Ads is the strongest pay-per-lead option — you pay per lead, get the Google Guaranteed badge, and capture high-intent searchers with close rates often between 20–40%. Among traditional marketplaces, Angi offers the most volume and Thumbtack the best controls for smaller jobs. But long term, the highest-ROI 'lead source' is an owned funnel you control rather than any marketplace you rent from.

faq.question: Are shared leads or exclusive leads better for contractors?
faq.answer: Exclusive leads close at meaningfully higher rates because you're not racing 3–5 competitors who bought the same contact. They cost more, but the math usually favors them for high-ticket trades. Shared leads can still work if priced accordingly and if you have fast, automated lead response — speed to first contact is the single biggest factor in winning a shared lead.

faq.question: How much do contractor leads cost?
faq.answer: It varies by trade and region, but shared marketplace leads typically run $30–$100 each, while exclusive and high-ticket leads (roofing, remodels, solar) can run $100–$300+. The number that matters more is cost-per-acquired-customer: at a 1-in-5 close rate, an $80 lead means roughly $400 to land a customer. Owned funnels usually start higher but drop well below that over 18–24 months as your database compounds.

faq.question: Should contractors use Angi and Thumbtack or build their own funnel?
faq.answer: Both — in sequence. Use marketplaces like Angi and Thumbtack to bridge cash flow and fill idle capacity while you build. Then invest in an owned funnel (conversion site, Google and Meta ads, a CRM with instant text-back, and reactivation campaigns) so you stop paying full price to reach the same homeowner twice. Cap marketplace spend as a percentage of revenue and shift the mix toward owned channels each quarter.

faq.question: How fast should you respond to a contractor lead?
faq.answer: Within 60 seconds if you can. Research consistently shows roughly 78% of customers buy from the company that responds first, and the odds of qualifying a lead drop sharply after the first five minutes. An automated SMS text-back through a CRM like GoHighLevel beats a competitor who calls back hours later, and it works on marketplace leads too.

articles.title: Best Lead Generation Companies for Contractors: Worth It?
articles.description: We break down the top pay-per-lead platforms for contractors, what they really cost over 24 months, and when building your own funnel wins.
articles.keyword: best lead generation companies for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Angi, HomeAdvisor, Thumbtack, Networx, CraftJack, Houzz Pro. If you've spent more than six months running a contracting business, you've cut a check to at least one of them. And if you're being honest, you've also stared at a $7,400 monthly invoice and wondered why your pipeline still feels thin. Here's the contrarian take most lead gen reviews won't give you: the best lead generation companies for contractors are excellent at one thing — getting you started. They are terrible at building enterprise value. After 24 months of renting leads, most contractors have spent $80K–$250K and own exactly zero of the customer relationships, search rankings, or brand equity that money produced. This article is for general contractors, roofers, HVAC operators, remodelers, and specialty trades doing $500K–$10M in revenue who are evaluating where to put their next marketing dollar. We'll rank the major pay-per-lead marketplaces, show the real math on long-term cost, and lay out when owning your funnel beats renting every time.

The pay-per-lead landscape in 2026

The marketplace model is simple: a platform aggregates homeowner demand through SEO, paid ads, and TV, then sells each inquiry to 3-5 contractors simultaneously. You pay $15-$150 per lead depending on trade and geography. Here are the players that actually matter for contractors: - Angi Leads (formerly HomeAdvisor): Largest inventory, lowest lead quality on average. Expect $20-$85 per shared lead. Close rates typically 4-8%.

  • Thumbtack: Better UX, mobile-first homeowner base. Leads run $15-$60. Skews smaller jobs ($500-$5K tickets).
  • Networx: Mid-tier volume, primarily roofing, HVAC, and plumbing. $25-$100 per lead.
  • CraftJack (Home Depot owned): Phone-verified leads, slightly higher quality. $30-$120 range.
  • Houzz Pro: Premium positioning, design-build and high-end remodel. Lower volume, higher ticket.
  • Modernize: Strong in solar, windows, roofing. Exclusive lead tier available for 2-3x the price. The newer entrants — Hatch, Service Direct, and 99 Calls — sell exclusive (not shared) leads at $80-$300 each. Quality is materially better, but you're now paying agency-level CPAs without the brand asset that comes with running your own ads.

What you're actually buying when you rent leads

Let's be precise about the product. A shared marketplace lead is a homeowner who filled out a form on someone else's website, and is being called by you and 3-4 competitors within 90 seconds. The economics work like this. Assume $45 per lead at a 6% close rate. That's $750 per acquired customer before you've paid a salesperson, a CSR, or done any follow-up. On a $12,000 roof, that's a 6.25% CAC — workable. On a $1,800 deck repair, it's 42% — catastrophic. Three things you are not buying: 1. The customer relationship. When that homeowner needs another service in 18 months, they go back to Angi. Not you. 2. The data. Angi keeps the search behavior, the email, the demographic profile. You get a name and phone number. 3. The brand impression. The homeowner thinks they hired "someone from Angi," not your company. Compare this to a Google Ads click that lands on your site, gets cookied, enters your email sequence in GoHighLevel or HubSpot, and is now a long-term asset on your balance sheet. Same dollar spent, completely different outcome.

The 24-month true cost of renting vs owning

I ran this model with a roofing client last quarter. Two-year horizon, $15K/month marketing budget. Here's how the numbers shake out. Scenario A — Pure marketplace spend:

  • $360K total spent across Angi + Networx + CraftJack
  • ~8,000 leads acquired at $45 blended
  • 6% close rate = 480 jobs
  • Zero owned audience at month 24
  • Cost per job: $750
  • Asset value created: $0 Scenario B — Owned funnel (Google Ads + Local Service Ads + SEO + retargeting):
  • $360K total spent (same budget)
  • Months 1-6: Higher CAC ($1,100/job) while SEO ramps
  • Months 7-24: CAC drops to $380/job as organic and repeat customers kick in
  • ~620 jobs over 24 months
  • Email list of ~4,200 past inquiries
  • Domain authority and ranking #1-3 for 15-25 local terms
  • Estimated asset value: $180K-$400K if you ever sell the business The owned-funnel scenario produces 29% more jobs at the same spend AND creates a sellable asset. The catch: it requires patience for 4-6 months and operational discipline most contractors don't have on day one. That's why marketplaces exist — they sell the shortcut, and the shortcut is real. It's just expensive.

When pay-per-lead marketplaces are the right call

I'm not anti-marketplace. They have a place. Use them when: - You're under 12 months old and have no domain authority, no Google reviews, no historical ad data. Marketplaces give you cash flow to survive while you build assets.

  • You're entering a new geo or service line and need to test demand before investing in localized SEO and ads.
  • You have idle crew capacity that you need to fill this week. Marketplace leads convert to revenue in 7-21 days. SEO converts in 90-180.
  • Your average ticket is above $8,000. The math forgives a $750 CAC when the gross margin is $4,000+. Don't use marketplaces when your ticket is under $3K, when your close rate on shared leads is below 5%, or when you've been on the platform for 18+ months and your CAC hasn't dropped. The platform isn't going to reward your tenure. It's an auction, and new bidders show up every quarter. The smart play: treat marketplaces as a tactical lever, not a strategy. Cap them at 30-40% of your lead volume. Anything higher and you're building someone else's business.

The owned-funnel stack that actually works for contractors

If you're going to build instead of rent, here's the stack I'd deploy for a $2M-$8M contractor today. It's not theoretical — this is what's working in 2026. Traffic layer:

  • Google Local Service Ads (LSAs): Pay-per-lead but you own the Google review profile. Run these first.
  • Google Search Ads on commercial-intent terms ("roof replacement [city]," "kitchen remodel near me")
  • Meta Ads for retargeting + lookalikes off your customer list. Not cold prospecting unless you have a strong creative team.
  • Local SEO through a Google Business Profile optimized weekly, plus 2-4 long-form service pages per month Conversion layer:
  • Landing pages built in Unbounce or Webflow, NOT your main site. One page per service per city.
  • Calendly or a GoHighLevel booking widget. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes or you lose 50% of the value.
  • A two-way SMS sequence triggered the moment a form fills. Nurture layer:
  • GoHighLevel or HubSpot CRM with a 12-touch email sequence over 90 days for unconverted leads
  • Quarterly newsletter to past customers — 20-30% of next-year revenue should come from this list
  • Review request automation immediately post-job completion Budget split for a $15K/month spend: $4K LSAs, $5K Google Search, $2K Meta retargeting, $2K SEO content, $2K tools and management.

How to evaluate any lead gen company before signing

If you're going to write checks to a third party — whether a marketplace or an agency — run them through this filter. I've used this with dozens of contractor clients and it kills bad deals fast. 1. Exclusivity. Are leads shared with competitors? If yes, your max acceptable CPL drops by 60%. 2. Attribution. Can they show you call recordings, form submissions, and source data in real-time? If they're hiding behind a dashboard with no raw data, walk. 3. Cancellation terms. Month-to-month or annual? Any contractor lead gen contract over 6 months is a red flag. 4. Lead replacement policy. What counts as a bad lead and what's the credit process? Get this in writing. 5. Geography and service match. Are you their 47th roofer in your zip code or their 3rd? Ask directly. 6. What happens at month 12. Will CPL go up, down, or stay flat? Get historical data from existing clients in similar markets. For agencies running your owned funnel, the questions shift: who owns the ad account, the domain, the CRM data, and the creative assets? Answer should be: you, you, you, and you. If any of those sit inside the agency's account, you're renting again — just with extra steps.

The hybrid model: rent to start, own to scale

The contractors I see win the long game don't pick a side. They run a deliberate 24-month transition. Months 1-6: 70% marketplace spend, 30% owned funnel build-out. Use marketplace cash flow to fund SEO content, ad testing, and CRM setup. Capture every marketplace lead's email and add to your nurture list (yes, this is allowed if you do the work). Months 7-12: 50/50 split. LSAs and Google Search should be matching marketplace volume by now at a lower CPA. If they're not, your landing pages or speed-to-lead are broken — fix those before adding more spend. Months 13-18: 30% marketplace, 70% owned. You should be ranking for 8-15 local terms and getting 40-60 organic inquiries per month. Marketplace becomes overflow capacity, not core volume. Months 19-24: 10-15% marketplace, 85% owned plus referrals. Marketplaces are now a tactical tool for slow weeks or new service launches, not a dependency. The contractors who skip this transition and stay 100% marketplace at year three are the ones who sell their business for 2x EBITDA instead of 5x. The buyer sees no defensible customer acquisition engine, and prices accordingly.

The bottom line

The best lead generation companies for contractors aren't actually the marketplaces — they're the platforms and channels you can own. Angi, Thumbtack, CraftJack, and the rest are useful tools for a specific stage of business, but they extract value that you should be compounding inside your own brand. Every dollar spent on a marketplace at year three is a dollar that didn't build an asset. Run the 24-month math on your own business. Pull your marketplace spend, divide by jobs closed, and compare to what the same money would do in LSAs + Google Search + SEO with a real CRM behind it. If the answer scares you, that's the signal to start the transition. Rent leads to survive, own the funnel to scale.

faq.question: Is Angi Leads worth it for contractors?
faq.answer: Angi can work in your first 12 months or as overflow capacity, but it's a poor long-term strategy. Expect 4-8% close rates on shared leads and CPAs around $600-$900 per closed job. Beyond 18 months on the platform, most contractors see flat or rising costs with no compounding return.

faq.question: How much should a contractor spend on lead generation?
faq.answer: A healthy benchmark is 6-12% of revenue for contractors under $5M, dropping to 4-7% as you scale and referrals/repeat business grow. Within that, no single channel — including marketplaces — should exceed 40% of total lead volume.

faq.question: What's the difference between shared and exclusive leads?
faq.answer: Shared leads are sold to 3-5 contractors simultaneously, so you're racing to call first. Exclusive leads come only to you, typically cost 2-4x more, and close at 15-25% versus 4-8% for shared. The math usually favors exclusive once your average ticket is above $5,000.

faq.question: Can I run Google Local Service Ads instead of using marketplaces?
faq.answer: Yes, and you probably should. LSAs are still pay-per-lead but you own the Google review profile, you appear at the top of search above marketplaces, and Google verifies the homeowner intent. CPLs typically run $25-$80 with materially better quality than shared marketplace leads.

faq.question: How long does it take to replace marketplace leads with my own funnel?
faq.answer: Plan for 6-9 months to match marketplace volume from owned channels, and 12-18 months to fully replace it at a lower blended CPA. The first 90 days are the hardest because SEO hasn't kicked in and you're paying to learn what ad creative and landing pages convert.

articles.title: Best CRM for Service Businesses: A 2026 Operator's Guide
articles.description: Speed-to-lead wins service deals. Here's how the best CRMs for service businesses actually compare on automation, pipeline, and ROI.
articles.keyword: Google Ads vs SEO for local business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most service businesses don't lose deals because their pricing is wrong. They lose deals because they take four hours to call a lead back. By then, the prospect has already booked the competitor who answered in five minutes.

That's the real job of a CRM for a service business: collapse the gap between "lead comes in" and "human makes contact" to near zero, then never let a follow-up fall through the cracks. Most owners buy a CRM for the wrong reason — they want a tidy contact database — and end up with expensive software nobody updates.

This guide ranks the leading options the way an operator evaluates them: speed-to-lead, pipeline visibility, automation depth, and total cost when you actually run it at scale. No feature checklists. Just what moves revenue.

Why speed-to-lead is the only metric that matters first

Lead-response research has been consistent for over a decade: contacting a web lead within five minutes makes you roughly 100x more likely to connect than waiting 30 minutes, and dramatically more likely to qualify them than waiting an hour. For a roofer, law firm, med spa, or HVAC company, that's the entire game.

A CRM earns its keep here in two ways. First, instant lead capture — the moment a form is submitted, a call comes in, or a Facebook lead ad fires, the record exists and a workflow triggers. Second, automated first touch: an SMS and email go out in seconds, and the rep gets a task or a ringless call connect before the lead cools.

When you evaluate any CRM, run one test: time how long it takes from "new lead" to "first automated text sent." If the platform can't do it in under 60 seconds without a paid Zapier middleman, it's not built for service businesses. Everything else — reporting, custom fields, integrations — is secondary to this single capability.

GoHighLevel: the operator's default for service businesses

For service businesses and the agencies that serve them, GoHighLevel (GHL) has become the default for a reason: it bundles the entire revenue stack into one bill. CRM, two-way SMS and email, calendars, pipelines, reputation/review requests, funnels, and a workflow builder that fires on form-fill, missed call, or pipeline-stage change.

The killer feature for service businesses is "missed-call text-back" — when someone calls and you don't pick up, an automated text goes out instantly so you don't lose them to the next listing. Pair that with appointment automations and review requests and you've replaced four separate tools.

The tradeoff is that GHL rewards setup. Out of the box it's a blank powerful engine; the ROI comes from building the automations correctly, which is exactly where most owners stall. It's also priced for businesses that will actually use the marketing stack — if you only want a contact list, it's overkill. But for a service business serious about speed-to-lead and follow-up at scale, nothing else consolidates this much for the money.

HubSpot: polished, scalable, and priced for it

HubSpot is the cleanest experience on the market. The free tier is genuinely useful, the interface is intuitive enough that a non-technical team will actually adopt it, and the reporting is best-in-class once you're on a paid Sales or Marketing Hub seat.

For a service business, HubSpot shines when you have a longer, more consultative sales cycle — think B2B services, consultancies, or higher-ticket professional firms where deals involve multiple touches and you need clean attribution from first click to closed-won. Sequences, deal pipelines, and native reporting are excellent.

The catch is cost curve. HubSpot is affordable to start and expensive to scale; marketing contacts, paid seats, and the jump between tiers add up fast once you're running real volume. It's also less SMS-native than GHL — texting and ringless voicemail usually mean a paid add-on or integration. If your team values polish and your deals are high-consideration, HubSpot is worth it. If you live and die on instant phone-and-text follow-up, the economics favor a more telephony-native platform.

Field service contenders: Jobber, Housecall Pro, ServiceTitan

If you dispatch technicians, a horizontal CRM isn't enough — you need scheduling, job costing, invoicing, and payments tied to the customer record. Three platforms dominate by company size.

Jobber suits small home-service teams (cleaning, landscaping, handyman). It's affordable, fast to set up, and handles quoting, scheduling, and invoicing without a steep learning curve. Housecall Pro sits a notch up, strong for plumbing, HVAC, and electrical, with better marketing automation, online booking, and consumer-financing options baked in.

ServiceTitan is the enterprise tier for serious trades shops doing real volume. It's powerful and deeply built for the trades — call booking, dispatch, capacity planning — but it's a major investment in both money and onboarding time, and it's overkill below roughly seven figures in revenue. The decision rule: pick the field-service platform for operations, but recognize that none of them match a dedicated marketing CRM for top-of-funnel lead nurture. Many growing shops run a field tool for ops plus GHL for marketing, synced together.
